proposedTopics.title: Audit Process & Methodology
proposedTopics.description: How a smart-contract security review actually runs, end to end: scoping the codebase, building a mental model before hunting bugs, and balancing manual review against tooling. This is the operating discipline the rest of Phase 6 (classification, tooling, fuzzing, reporting) assumes.

proposedTopics.title: Severity & Vulnerability Classification
proposedTopics.description: The frameworks that turn 'this looks bad' into defensible analysis: the OWASP Smart Contract Top 10 (2026) for risk categories, Immunefi's impact-led scale with likelihood downgrade factors for bounty severity, and the EEA EthTrust levels for certification — plus why the unmaintained SWC registry needs current supporting guidance.

proposedTopics.title: Static Analysis Tooling
proposedTopics.description: Static analyzers inspect source and compiler representations without executing generated transaction sequences. Slither provides detectors and code-comprehension printers; Aderyn produces Markdown, JSON, and SARIF reports and supports editor integration. Their output is evidence to triage, not a substitute for manual protocol reasoning.

proposedTopics.title: Fuzzing & Invariants for Security
proposedTopics.description: Where static analysis stops, dynamic testing over random/guided call sequences picks up: Foundry's built-in invariant testing, Echidna, and Medusa all hammer a contract with call sequences looking for a property that should always hold to break. The hard part isn't running the fuzzer — it's writing invariants specific enough to catch a real bug.

proposedTopics.title: Security Report Writing
proposedTopics.description: Turning findings into a report a client, a bounty payout, or a public disclosure can act on: justifying the severity you assigned against a named framework, keeping the proof of concept as small as possible while still convincing, and writing recommendations specific enough to implement without another meeting.

proposedTopics.title: Reading an unfamiliar codebase
proposedTopics.description: Auditing starts by orienting, not reading top-to-bottom: find every external/public entry point, trace which ones move value or change privileged state, and sketch a call graph of who calls whom before hunting for bugs. A codebase read in file order hides the actual attack surface, which is defined by reachability from an attacker-controlled call, not by file layout.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: pick any contract in security/samples/, and in security/notes/<contract>-entrypoints.md list every external/public function, mark which ones move value or change access-control state, and draw a one-page call graph. Done when: the notes file names at least one function you would NOT have flagged as security-relevant on a top-to-bottom read.

requirements.purpose: Map attacker-reachable state-changing entry points, authorization, and call relationships before review

options.title: Slither README
options.scope: Sections Usage and Printers, including entry-points, call-graph, and vars-and-auth
options.why: The official tool reference provides the exact entry-point, call-graph, and authorization printers that make the learner's manual map complete and checkable.

proposedTopics.title: Audit scoping & the audit lifecycle
proposedTopics.description: A scope pins down exactly what's being reviewed before work starts: a commit hash (not a moving branch), a list of in-scope files/contracts, known issues excluded up front, and a fixed time window. The lifecycle then runs scoping → initial review → findings drafted → fix review (re-checking patches against the same commit range) → final report — skipping fix review is how 'fixed' bugs ship half-fixed.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in security/notes/scope-template.md, write a scope document for a sample protocol in security/samples/ — commit hash, in-scope file list, out-of-scope/known-issues, and lifecycle stages with target dates. Done when: the template has a named commit-hash field and a distinct 'fix review' stage separate from the initial review.

requirements.purpose: Freeze the exact review target and distinguish initial review, fix review, and final delivery

options.title: What Is a Smart Contract Audit, the OpenZeppelin Way
options.scope: Sections Audit Preparation & Scope Definition, Reporting & Fix Review, and Final Delivery & Optional Publication
options.why: OpenZeppelin's current process pins the codebase and commit hash, verifies fixes against the whole codebase, and distinguishes the initial report from final delivery after fix review.

proposedTopics.title: Note-taking and building a mental model
proposedTopics.description: Good audit notes aren't a transcript of the code — they're an evolving model of invariants ('X should never exceed Y') and open questions ('what happens if this reverts mid-loop?') tagged to specific lines, so a two-line hunch survives to become a real finding a week later. Auditors who don't write down assumptions re-derive (or forget) them every time they revisit a file.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: while reviewing a sample contract in security/samples/, keep running notes in security/notes/<contract>-model.md: a list of invariants you believe hold plus a separate list of open questions/hunches with file:line references. Done when: you have at least 3 invariants and 2 open questions, each pointing at the exact line it depends on.

requirements.purpose: Turn system assumptions and high-value state-machine behavior into explicit review properties and questions

options.title: Building Secure Contracts: Program Analysis
options.scope: Sections Determining Security Properties and Components
options.why: The maintained Trail of Bits guide shows how threat modeling, state machines, access control, arithmetic, and external interactions become concrete properties rather than code paraphrase.

proposedTopics.title: Manual review vs. automated tooling
proposedTopics.description: Static analyzers quickly match structural bug patterns, while fuzzers execute generated call sequences against explicit properties; neither can decide whether an unstated business rule is correct. A competent review runs tools early for the checks they can express, then spends human time defining protocol intent and reasoning about business logic and cross-contract behavior.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: on a sample contract in security/samples/, run one static analyzer (see the Static Analysis Tooling chapter) and separately do a 20-minute manual read; in security/notes/manual-vs-tool.md classify every observation as tool-only, manual-only, or both, leaving a column empty with a note if the exercise produced no such observation. Done when: every actual tool result and manual observation is classified without inventing an example to fill a column.

requirements.purpose: Choose static analysis, fuzzing, and manual reasoning according to their documented strengths and limits

The ordering is primarily driven by practitioner survey mean rank, with incident evidence used to validate it.

Done when: you can recite the top 4 in order without looking and explain from OWASP's methodology why reentrancy is ranked eighth.

proposedTopics.title: Immunefi severity classification
proposedTopics.description: Immunefi's classification system grades a bug largely by the consequence of a successful exploit. Smart-contract examples include Critical for direct theft or permanent freezing of funds, High for theft of unclaimed yield or temporary freezing, Medium for griefing with no profit motive, and Low when a contract fails to deliver promised returns without losing value. Elevated privileges or uncommon user interaction may downgrade or disqualify a report.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in security/notes/immunefi-severity.md, classify 4 hypothetical bugs (invent them, or pull from security/samples/) against Critical/High/Medium/Low using Immunefi's impact-first criteria, and note one case where likelihood (e.g. requires a compromised owner key) would downgrade it. Done when: each of your 4 has a one-line impact justification citing the Immunefi tier criterion it matches.

requirements.purpose: Classify blockchain and smart-contract impacts and apply documented likelihood downgrade factors

options.title: Immunefi Vulnerability Severity Classification System v2.3
options.scope: Sections Blockchain/DLT and Smart Contracts, plus the opening classification guidance
options.why: Immunefi's canonical scale defines the four impact-led tiers and explicitly explains downgrades for elevated privilege or uncommon user interaction.

proposedTopics.title: EEA EthTrust levels & the SWC registry's retirement
proposedTopics.description: The current EEA EthTrust Security Levels specification defines three cumulative certification tiers: [S] focuses on checks usually suitable for automated static analysis, [M] adds stricter checks requiring human judgment, and [Q] adds documented functional-correctness and business-logic review. The SWC registry says it has not been thoroughly updated since 2020 and may contain errors or omissions, so a bare SWC identifier needs current supporting guidance.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in security/notes/ethtrust-vs-swc.md, write 3–4 sentences explaining what each EthTrust level adds over the one below it, and why citing a bare 'SWC-107' in a 2026 finding is a red flag rather than good practice. Done when: you can name what changes between the lowest and highest EthTrust tier (automated checks vs documented functional-correctness review) without re-reading the spec.

requirements.purpose: Compare the cumulative S, M, and Q certification requirements in the current EthTrust release

options.title: EEA EthTrust Security Levels Specification Version 3
options.scope: Sections 2 Conformance and 5 EEA EthTrust Security Levels
options.why: The current March 2025 EEA specification is the normative source for cumulative conformance and the S, M, and Q requirements; it supersedes the legacy v1 link.

requirements.purpose: Verify why a bare SWC identifier is insufficient current vulnerability guidance

proposedTopics.title: Anatomy of a good finding
proposedTopics.description: A finding a client can act on uses a descriptive title, a clear vulnerability and impact explanation, explicit risk reasoning, a runnable proof of concept, and a recommendation specific enough to implement. Vague findings get deprioritized because the reader cannot reproduce the issue or determine what is actually at stake.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: pick one bug you found (or seed one) in a security/samples/ contract and write it up in security/reports/finding-01.md with Title, Bug Description, Impact, Risk Breakdown, Recommendation, and Proof of Concept sections. Done when: the title names the vulnerability and impact, the PoC is runnable, and the recommendation names a concrete fix or mitigation.

requirements.purpose: Write a concise finding with reproducible impact, runnable proof, and a specific mitigation

proposedTopics.title: Slither static analysis
proposedTopics.description: Slither is Trail of Bits' Python-based static-analysis framework: it compiles Solidity or Vyper, builds the SlithIR intermediate representation, runs vulnerability detectors, and offers printers for entry points, call graphs, inheritance, and authorization. Its official CLI integrates with Foundry and Hardhat projects, but every emitted detector result still needs code-specific triage.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: run `slither .` against a sample contract in security/samples/ and save the raw output to security/notes/slither-output.txt; then in security/notes/slither-triage.md classify each finding as real or false-positive with a one-line reason. Done when: every emitted finding is classified as a true or false positive with a one-line code-specific reason.

requirements.purpose: Run Slither on a Foundry or Hardhat project and interpret detector impact and confidence

options.title: Slither README
options.scope: Sections Features, Usage, and Detectors
options.why: The maintained official README provides the exact project command, detector catalogue, and impact/confidence metadata needed to run and triage output.

proposedTopics.title: Aderyn static analysis
proposedTopics.description: Aderyn is Cyfrin's Rust-based Solidity static analyzer. It supports Foundry and Hardhat projects without configuration, produces Markdown, JSON, or SARIF reports, and powers an official VS Code extension. Comparing its report with Slither exposes overlap and differences without assuming in advance that either tool must find a unique issue.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: run `aderyn` on the same sample contract you ran Slither on, save the report, and in security/notes/slither-vs-aderyn.md list which findings appeared in both tools, which appeared in only one, and any clear false positive from either. Done when: every finding from both reports appears in the overlap/tool-only comparison, even if one tool has no unique finding.

requirements.purpose: Run Aderyn with its current CLI and compare its report against Slither without assuming unique findings

options.scope: Sections What is Aderyn, Features, and Quick Start
options.why: Cyfrin's maintained README defines current Foundry/Hardhat support, report formats, and the bare `aderyn` command; it avoids the stale `aderyn .` invocation.

proposedTopics.title: What static analysis catches vs misses
proposedTopics.description: Static tools can flag detector-defined syntactic and structural patterns without generated execution, but their approximations can produce false alarms and miss bugs outside the encoded checks. Protocol-specific intent must still be supplied through manual reasoning or explicit properties for dynamic analysis. Treat tool output as a prioritized list to investigate, not a verdict.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in security/notes/tool-limits.md, write down (from your own Slither/Aderyn runs) one true positive, one suspected false positive if present, and one protocol-specific property not expressed by either tool, with a one-sentence reason for each. Done when: every entry references an actual finding, tool output, or contract you inspected rather than inventing a required false positive.

requirements.purpose: Distinguish detector output, false alarms, and protocol-specific security properties requiring other analysis

options.title: Building Secure Contracts: Program Analysis
options.scope: Sections Program Analysis comparison table, Suggested Workflow, and Determining Security Properties
options.why: Trail of Bits explicitly documents static analysis speed, possible false alarms, moderate misses, and the need to define higher-level state-machine properties for fuzzing or manual review.

proposedTopics.title: Foundry invariant testing
proposedTopics.description: Foundry invariant tests run generated sequences of calls against targeted contracts and re-check `invariant_` properties as the sequence advances. A handler is an intentional layer for constraining actions and tracking ghost state, not a requirement of every campaign. A failing run reports the call sequence that broke the property.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in test/security/invariant/SampleInvariant.t.sol, write a Foundry invariant test with a handler contract for a sample contract in security/samples/, asserting one real property (e.g. sum of balances == totalSupply) and setting explicit runs and depth. Done when: `forge test --match-contract SampleInvariant` completes those campaign settings with zero invariant violations, and you can explain what the handler restricts the fuzzer to calling.

requirements.purpose: Build a targeted stateful invariant campaign with handler actions, ghost accounting, and configured runs and depth

options.title: Foundry Invariant Testing
options.scope: Sections Invariant Testing overview, Handler pattern, Ghost variables, and Configuring invariant runs
options.why: The current official Foundry guide covers stateful call sequences, handler targeting, ghost-variable accounting, and campaign configuration used by the learner's test.

proposedTopics.title: Echidna property-based fuzzing
proposedTopics.description: Echidna is Trail of Bits' property-based smart-contract fuzzer: you write properties as no-argument Solidity functions returning a bool with an `echidna` prefix, or use its assertion testing mode, then point Echidna at the target contract so it can generate call sequences looking for a failure.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: write an `echidna_` property function for the same sample contract you invariant-tested in Foundry, in security/samples/EchidnaSample.sol, and run `echidna security/samples/EchidnaSample.sol --contract EchidnaSample`. Done when: Echidna reports the property held for the bounded campaign or prints a failing call sequence that you can explain.

options.why: Trail of Bits' maintained tutorial defines property signatures, state-discard semantics during property evaluation, target selection, and the exact CLI exercised by the build.

proposedTopics.title: Medusa parallel fuzzing
proposedTopics.description: Medusa is a Go, go-ethereum-based smart-contract fuzzer inspired by Echidna. It runs property and assertion campaigns across parallel workers, retains coverage-increasing call sequences in a corpus, and mutates that corpus to guide exploration. Its concurrency makes worker count and tool-specific metrics important context for any benchmark.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: configure medusa.json for the same sample contract, run `medusa fuzz`, and in security/notes/echidna-vs-medusa.md record the fixed time window, worker count, and each tool's reported test-call or sequence metric. Done when: you can compare the reported metrics while clearly naming that they are tool-specific rather than assuming identical test-case units.

requirements.purpose: Configure and run Medusa's parallel coverage-guided campaign and interpret its reported metrics carefully

options.why: The official maintained repository defines worker parallelism, coverage-guided corpus behavior, and supported property/assertion modes; its linked first-party First Steps page provides `medusa init`, `medusa.json`, and `medusa fuzz` execution.

proposedTopics.title: Writing good invariants
proposedTopics.description: A good invariant states something that must be true after ANY sequence of allowed calls, in terms an attacker can't route around — 'totalSupply equals the sum of balances', 'a user can never withdraw more than they deposited', 'share price is monotonically non-decreasing except on explicit loss events'. A weak invariant either restates something trivially true regardless of bugs, or is so narrow it only covers the one path you already checked by hand — the fuzzer can only find what your invariant is capable of catching.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: for a sample contract in security/samples/, write 2 invariants in test/security/invariant/ — one about conservation of value (e.g. sum-of-parts equals total) and one about an access-control property (e.g. only role X ever changes Y) — and run both with explicit campaign settings. Done when: you can explain, for each, a bug that WOULD violate it and one that WOULD NOT (its blind spot).

requirements.purpose: Design conservation and access-control properties with explicit security meaning and blind spots

proposedTopics.title: Stateful vs stateless fuzzing
proposedTopics.description: Stateless fuzzing resets state between generated transactions, which suits properties that can be checked from one call against the initial state. Stateful fuzzing preserves state across a sequence, so it can reach and test properties that depend on accumulated state or several transactions in a specific order.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in security/notes/stateless-vs-stateful.md, take one bug class you can only trigger with 2+ ordered transactions (e.g. deposit, then a state-changing call, then withdraw) and explain why a stateless fuzz test on any single function couldn't have found it. Done when: you can name the exact 2nd/3rd call your stateless test would be missing.

requirements.purpose: Explain state reset and multi-call reachability differences between stateless and stateful fuzz campaigns

options.scope: Section Stateless vs. Stateful, including Recommendations
options.why: Trail of Bits directly defines default stateful behavior, `--seqLen 1` stateless behavior, reset semantics, and why ordered-operation bugs can be hidden.

proposedTopics.title: Severity justification in reports
proposedTopics.description: A severity rating without justification is an opinion; citing the exact Immunefi impact criterion you matched, plus the concrete preconditions (does it need a privileged role, a specific market condition, or just a normal user call?), turns 'High' into something a reviewer can check and disagree with on the merits. The justification is also where you note anything that could downgrade or disqualify an impact-only read, including required privilege or uncommon user interaction.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: take one finding from security/reports/ (or write a new one) and add a 'Severity justification' section naming the exact tier criterion matched and any precondition that affects it. Done when: another reader, given only your justification section, would assign the same tier without seeing the rest of the report.

requirements.purpose: Justify a report severity with a named impact criterion and explicit exploit preconditions

proposedTopics.title: Writing a minimal PoC
proposedTopics.description: A minimal proof of concept is the smallest Foundry test that reproduces the bug end to end — one setup, the exact call sequence that triggers it, and an assertion showing the bad outcome (funds moved, invariant broken) — with every unrelated setup step, mock, or helper stripped out. Padding a PoC with the whole protocol's deployment script obscures the one thing that matters: what a reviewer must change to make the assertion fail again.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: for the finding you wrote up in security/reports/, add a Foundry test at test/security/poc/Finding01PoC.t.sol that reproduces it in the fewest lines you can manage, asserting the concrete bad outcome. Done when: `forge test --match-contract Finding01PoC` passes while asserting the exploit succeeds on the vulnerable contract, then fails or changes to the expected safe outcome after the fix, with no unrelated setup left.

requirements.purpose: Produce a runnable, bounded proof that demonstrates the concrete exploit outcome without unrelated setup

options.title: How to Submit Bug Reports That Get Paid
options.scope: Section Proof of Concept
options.why: Immunefi explicitly requires runnable exploit code rather than pseudocode or steps and accepts Foundry tests as a valid PoC form.

proposedTopics.title: Actionable recommendations
proposedTopics.description: A recommendation a developer can act on names the specific change or mitigation, such as adding a guard to `withdraw`, reordering an external call and state update, or validating an amount before transfer, rather than restating a general principle with no pointer to the affected code.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: for the same finding, write the Recommendation section in security/reports/finding-01.md naming the exact function or line to change, the specific fix or mitigation, and how it prevents the PoC outcome. Done when: a developer can identify the code change and rerun the PoC to verify the mitigation.

requirements.purpose: Write a specific mitigation tied to the affected code and disclose relevant tradeoffs

options.title: How to Submit Bug Reports That Get Paid
options.scope: Sections Recommendation and Proof of Concept
options.why: Immunefi's reporting guide requires a fix or impact mitigation and connects it to a runnable exploit, keeping the recommendation concrete and verifiable.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Why does an auditor start from entry points and value flow instead of reading a contract top to bottom?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Attack surface is defined by what an attacker can reach and influence — external/public functions and the state they touch — not by source order; starting there finds the reachable bugs fastest and builds the mental model (who can call what, who can move funds) that later line-by-line reading hangs onto. Pitfall: a function with no external caller in this codebase can still be reachable via a delegatecall, a proxy, or another contract you haven't looked at yet.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What does pinning an audit's scope to a commit hash (not a branch) protect against, and what does the 'fix review' stage catch that the initial review can't?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: A commit hash freezes exactly what was reviewed — a moving branch means new, unreviewed code could ship under the audit's name. Fix review re-checks that a proposed patch to a finding actually closes the hole and didn't introduce a new one, which the initial review (written before any fix existed) structurally cannot do. Pitfall: reviewing a fix in isolation, without re-running it against the rest of the in-scope code, misses fixes that break an invariant elsewhere.

proposedPrompts.topicTitle: Note-taking and building a mental model
proposedPrompts.promptText: What should audit notes capture beyond a paraphrase of the code, and why?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Invariants ('balance never exceeds totalSupply'), trust assumptions ('caller is assumed to be the router'), and open questions, each tagged to a file:line — because a finding is usually a violated invariant you noticed days earlier, and without a note it gets lost when you move to the next file. Pitfall: notes without a line reference become unverifiable later — you'll re-read the whole file to confirm what you meant.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What kind of bug can a human auditor catch that no static analyzer or fuzzer can, and why?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: A business-logic error where the code runs exactly as written but implements the wrong economic rule (e.g. a reward formula that pays out a token nobody put in) — there's no crash, no violated pattern, and no property to check against, because 'correct' behavior only exists in a human's understanding of the protocol's intent. Pitfall: don't skip tooling either — humans are slow and inconsistent at the mechanical pattern-matching tools do well.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Where does Reentrancy rank in the OWASP Smart Contract Top 10 (2026), and what pushed it there?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: SC08. OWASP's methodology says the 2026 order is primarily driven by practitioner survey mean rank, with 2025 incident data and qualitative input used to validate the result; the published sources do not reduce the placement to a single loss-total explanation. Pitfall: a lower rank is an awareness priority, not evidence that an individual reentrancy finding is low severity.

proposedPrompts.promptText: How does Immunefi's system decide severity, and what can override an impact-based rating?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Immunefi classifies largely by successful-exploit impact. Smart-contract examples include Critical for direct theft or permanent freezing of funds, High for theft of unclaimed yield or temporary freezing, Medium for griefing without profit motive, and Low when promised returns fail without value loss. Elevated privileges or uncommon user interaction may downgrade or disqualify a report. Pitfall: use the exact table entry and the program's in-scope impacts, not these examples as an exhaustive tier definition.

proposedPrompts.topicTitle: EEA EthTrust levels & the SWC registry's retirement
proposedPrompts.promptText: Why is SWC-1xx numbering considered stale in a 2026 audit report, and what should replace it?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: The SWC registry says it has not been thoroughly updated since 2020 and may contain errors and crucial omissions. Keep an SWC ID only as a legacy cross-reference and support the finding with current maintained guidance such as the EEA EthTrust requirements or another current standard that actually defines the issue. Pitfall: old templates and tool output can still emit SWC IDs; that does not make the registry current.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What are the four parts of a well-formed audit finding, in order, and what does each have to do?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Title names the vulnerability and impact; Bug Description explains the issue clearly; Impact and Risk Breakdown quantify the consequence and exploitation difficulty; Recommendation gives a concrete fix or mitigation; Proof of Concept supplies runnable exploit code. Pitfall: steps or pseudocode can supplement a report but do not replace the runnable PoC Immunefi requires.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Enter one CodeHawks First Flight and write up your best finding using the title/impact/PoC/recommendation structure.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Register for an active beginner-friendly contest, scope-read the protocol using this chapter's process, and produce one finding write-up (even a Low) in the four-part structure — the real judge here is your report's clarity, not whether you find a Critical.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What does Slither analyze to find bugs, and what's the tradeoff of that approach?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: It parses and compiles the source into an AST/IR (SlithIR) and pattern-matches known-bad shapes across it — no execution, so it's fast and scales to large codebases, but it can only flag shapes it has a detector for, and doesn't know what the code is supposed to do (business logic), only how it's structured. Pitfall: a clean Slither run means 'no known pattern matched', not 'this contract is safe'.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Why run both Slither and Aderyn on the same codebase instead of just one?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: They are independently maintained analyzers with their own detector catalogues and report formats, so comparing both outputs can reveal overlap or differences on the code under review. Do not assume each must find a unique bug: record the complete union and triage every result. Pitfall: the same finding from both tools is duplicate evidence to investigate, not automatic confirmation of severity.

proposedPrompts.topicTitle: What static analysis catches vs misses
proposedPrompts.promptText: Name a bug class static analyzers structurally cannot catch, and explain why.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: A business-logic error where the code is syntactically valid but implements the wrong protocol rule, such as an incorrect reward split, can fall outside detector-defined checks because the intended rule was never encoded. Supply that intent through manual review or an explicit property for dynamic analysis. Pitfall: static analysis can also raise false alarms, so every result still needs code-specific triage.

proposedPrompts.promptText: How does a Foundry invariant test differ from an ordinary fuzz test, and what is the handler contract for?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: A fuzz test exercises one test function with generated inputs; an invariant campaign generates sequences of calls and repeatedly checks `invariant_` properties, so it can expose order-dependent state bugs. A handler is an optional targeted layer that constrains actions and tracks ghost state for complex systems. Pitfall: unrealistic handler actions can break a property in a state no real caller can reach.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Sketch the shape of a Foundry invariant test asserting totalSupply equals the sum of tracked balances.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: contract Handler { Vault v; constructor(Vault _v) { v = _v; } function deposit(uint256 x) external { v.deposit(x); } } contract VaultInvariant is Test { Handler h; Vault v; function setUp() external { v = new Vault(); h = new Handler(v); targetContract(address(h)); } function invariant_solvency() external { assertEq(v.totalSupply(), v.trackedSum()); } }

proposedPrompts.promptText: How does Echidna decide a property has failed, and what does it do once it finds a failing sequence?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: In property mode, an `echidna`-prefixed function takes no arguments and must return true; Echidna reports a generated transaction sequence that makes it return false or revert and attempts to shrink the sequence. Property-call side effects are discarded, so the function need not be a pure read, but test properties should remain separate from production behavior. Assertion mode instead looks for failing Solidity assertions.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write an Echidna property function checking total supply never exceeds a fixed cap.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: function echidna_supply_never_exceeds_cap() public view returns (bool) { return token.totalSupply() <= CAP; }

proposedPrompts.promptText: What does Medusa add over Echidna, mechanically, and what do they share?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: They share the same property/assertion-testing model (test-writing style is nearly identical), but Medusa parallelizes fuzzing workers across CPU cores and uses branch-coverage guidance to steer exploration toward unexplored code paths, aiming for higher throughput on multi-core hardware; being Go/go-ethereum-based also gives it a native API for embedding in other tools. Pitfall: more executions per second only helps if your invariants are good — a fast fuzzer restating a weak property just finds nothing, faster.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What separates a strong security invariant from a weak one?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Strong: a global property (conservation of value, an access-control boundary, a monotonicity guarantee) that any sequence of allowed calls must preserve, expressed independently of how you think the exploit would happen. Weak: something trivially true by construction (so it can never fail regardless of bugs) or scoped so narrowly it only re-checks the one code path you already manually verified. Pitfall: an invariant referencing implementation details (a specific internal variable name) breaks the moment you refactor, even with no behavior change.

proposedPrompts.promptText: When is a stateless fuzz test enough, and when do you need stateful (sequence) fuzzing instead?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Stateless mode is appropriate for a property of one call from reset state, such as pure math or an encoder/decoder round-trip. Use stateful mode when reachability depends on accumulated state or ordered calls, such as deposit → state change → withdraw. Pitfall: passing stateless tests do not cover multi-call ordering bugs, while stateful campaigns still cover only the properties and reachable actions you supply.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What makes a severity rating defensible rather than just asserted?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Citing the specific criterion of a named framework (e.g. Immunefi 'permanent freezing of funds' = Critical) plus the concrete preconditions required to trigger it (privileged role needed? normal user call? specific market state?) — a bare 'Critical' with no framework reference or precondition analysis can't be checked or disputed on the merits. Pitfall: omitting a precondition that would downgrade severity (e.g. 'only exploitable if the owner key is already compromised') overstates the real risk.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What is a minimal PoC trying to isolate, and what's the test for whether you've minimized enough?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: It isolates the exact precondition, call sequence, and observable bad outcome that proves the bug, stripped of unrelated setup. The exploit test should pass on vulnerable code while asserting that bad outcome; after the fix, the exploit should revert or the assertion should change to the expected safe outcome. Pitfall: removing a real attacker precondition merely to shorten the PoC overstates reachability.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What separates an actionable recommendation from a generic one?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Actionable: names the exact function or line, gives a specific fix or impact mitigation, and explains how it blocks the reproduced outcome. Generic: restates a principle such as 'follow CEI' without pointing to the affected code, leaving the developer to derive the change. Pitfall: verify the recommendation against the runnable PoC; plausible prose alone does not show that the impact is mitigated.

proposedPrompts.topicTitle: The Solodit checklist as a working reference
proposedPrompts.promptText: What is the Solodit checklist, and where does it fit relative to your own manual review and static analysis?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: A checklist of known audit findings/checks aggregated from real contests and reports, organized by category — it's a last-pass safety net for known patterns, not a replacement for reasoning about this specific protocol's business logic (which tools and checklists both structurally can't cover). Pitfall: running the checklist first and skipping your own mental-model read produces a report that only reflects what's already been seen before — genuinely novel bugs need the earlier chapters' process, not a checklist.

proposedPrompts.topicTitle: The Solodit checklist as a working reference
proposedPrompts.promptText: Work through the Solodit checklist against one contract you've reviewed this phase and log every match.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Pick a category (e.g. access control, oracle usage) relevant to your sample contract, walk its checks one by one, and record hits/misses in security/notes/solodit-pass.md — treat any hit your manual pass missed as a gap in your mental model to close.
